01.note: A pious man was praying by the road when an officer greeted him. He did not answer, and the officer waited until he finished, then called him a good-for-nothing: his own Torah tells him to guard his life, and the officer could have cut off his head with a sword and no one would have held him to account. The pious man asked what would happen to someone who stopped to return a friend's greeting while standing before a human king; the officer said they would cut off his head. The pious man answered that he had been standing before the King of kings, who lives forever, so all the more so he could not stop. The officer was appeased, and the pious man went home in peace.
01.why: The discussion is about whether one may break off prayer to answer a ruler's greeting; Rav Yosef has just said one must interrupt for a gentile king because of the danger. This pious man refused to interrupt for a gentile officer and came through unharmed.

people.name: the pious man
people.about: A man praying by the road who will not stop his prayer to return an officer's greeting

people.name: the officer
people.about: A gentile official who greets the praying man and is angered when he gets no reply

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if something holds for a mortal king, it holds all the more for God.

terms.term: the Holy One, Blessed be He
terms.meaning: A common Talmudic name for God.

02.note: A creature called an arvad was harming people in one place, and they came to tell Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa. He asked to be shown its hole and put his heel over the opening; the arvad came out, bit him, and died. He carried it on his shoulder to the study hall and told those there: it is not the arvad that kills, it is sin that kills. At that moment the Sages said: woe to the man an arvad attacks, and woe to the arvad that Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa attacks.
02.why: The discussion is about which dangers justify stopping in the middle of prayer, building on the mishna's rule that one does not stop even if a snake is wrapped around one's heel. This story shows a righteous man whom even a deadly creature could not harm.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage the people turn to for help against the creature; it bites him and dies

terms.meaning: A dangerous biting creature, some kind of venomous reptile; the translation leaves the word untranslated.
The house of study where the Sages and their students gathered to learn Torah.

03.note: A man leading the prayers in front of Rabba added the line: You have shown mercy to the bird's nest, now have mercy and pity on us. Rabba praised him: how well this scholar knows how to appease his Master. Abaye objected that the mishna says such a prayer leader is silenced.
03.why: The mishna says a prayer leader who invokes God's mercy to the bird's nest is silenced, and two Sages have just argued over why. The Gemara then explains that Rabba agreed with the mishna and only praised the man to sharpen Abaye's mind.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage in whose presence the man leads prayer; he praises the added line

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects to Rabba that the mishna says such a leader is silenced

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.
The Torah's command to send away the mother bird before taking her eggs or chicks, read here as a sign of God's mercy.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and explains.

04.note: A man leading the prayers in front of Rabbi Hanina piled on praises of God: great, mighty, awesome, powerful, strong, fearless, steadfast, honored and more. Rabbi Hanina waited until he finished and then asked whether he had now completed all his Master's praises. Even the three words we do say, great, mighty and awesome, we could not say had Moses not written them in the Torah and the Men of the Great Assembly not put them into the prayer. It is like praising a king who owns thousands of gold coins for having silver ones: an insult, not an honor.
04.why: The mishna has listed innovations in prayer that get a prayer leader silenced. This story follows as another case of a prayer leader corrected for adding to the set wording of the Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who rebukes a prayer leader for adding a long string of praises of God

people.name: Moses
people.about: Cited by Rabbi Hanina as the one who first said the words great, mighty and awesome in the Torah

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.
An early council of Sages credited with fixing the wording of the prayers.
The central standing prayer of Jewish worship, recited several times a day.

05.note: A student led the prayers in front of Rabbi Eliezer and dragged the prayer on far too long. Rabbi Eliezer's students complained: how long-winded he is! Rabbi Eliezer answered: is he going on any longer than Moses, who prayed forty days and forty nights?
05.why: The Gemara has been discussing the structure of the Amida prayer and where personal requests belong. This story, paired with the next one about a very short prayer, shows Rabbi Eliezer allowing a prayer to be as long as the one praying needs.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who defends a student whose prayer runs very long

people.name: Moses
people.about: Cited by Rabbi Eliezer for praying forty days and forty nights

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.

06.note: Another time a student led the prayers in front of Rabbi Eliezer and cut the prayer far too short. Rabbi Eliezer's students protested: how brief he is! Rabbi Eliezer answered: is he any briefer than Moses, who prayed for his sister Miriam with only the words: Please, God, heal her, please?
06.why: It pairs with the story just before it, where Rabbi Eliezer defended a very long prayer; together they show he accepted both. The Gemara then learns from Moses' short prayer that one praying for someone else need not mention the person's name.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who defends a student whose prayer is very short

people.name: Moses
people.about: Cited by Rabbi Eliezer for his five-word prayer to heal Miriam

people.name: Miriam
people.about: Moses' sister, for whose healing he prayed

terms.meaning: Served as the leader of communal prayer, who stood before the cabinet holding the Torah scrolls.

07.note: Rabban Gamliel's son fell ill, and he sent two scholars to ask Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to pray for him. Rabbi Hanina went up to his attic, prayed, came down and told them to go, because the fever had left the boy. Asked if he was a prophet, he said no, but he had a tradition: if his prayer flows fluently from his mouth, he knows it was accepted; if not, it was rejected. The scholars wrote down the exact moment. When they came back, Rabban Gamliel swore by the Temple service that they had it exactly: at that very hour the fever broke and the boy asked for water.
07.why: The mishna mentions Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa and his sign that a fluent prayer is an accepted one; the Gemara follows with stories of how his prayers worked.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Father of the sick boy; he sends scholars to ask Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to pray

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage whose prayer heals the boy; he knows it was accepted by how fluently it came

terms.meaning: An oath formula: Rabban Gamliel swears by the worship once performed in the Temple in Jerusalem.

08.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa went to study Torah with Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai, whose son fell ill. Rabbi Yohanan asked him to pray for the boy so that he would live. Rabbi Hanina put his head between his knees, prayed, and the boy lived. Rabbi Yohanan said that if he himself had kept his head between his knees all day, Heaven would have paid him no attention. His wife asked: is Hanina greater than you? He said no, but Hanina is like a servant before the King, and he is like a minister before the King.
08.why: The mishna mentions Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's power in prayer; this is the second of the Gemara's stories showing it, after the healing of Rabban Gamliel's son.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai whose prayer saves his teacher's son

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Hanina's teacher; his son falls ill and he asks Hanina to pray

people.name: his wife
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai's wife, who asks whether Hanina is greater than he is

09.note: Rabban Gamliel and the Sages were dining in an upper room in Jericho and were served dates. Rabban Gamliel gave Rabbi Akiva the honor of leading the blessing afterward, and Rabbi Akiva quickly recited a single blessing that sums up the three of the Grace after Meals. Rabban Gamliel said: Akiva, how long will you keep sticking your head into disputes? Rabbi Akiva answered: our teacher, you say one thing and your colleagues say another, but you yourself taught us that when one disagrees with many, the law follows the many.
09.why: The Gemara has just cited a dispute: for foods of the seven species, Rabban Gamliel requires the full three blessings of Grace after Meals, while the Rabbis say one abridged blessing is enough. Here Rabbi Akiva follows the Rabbis in front of Rabban Gamliel himself.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The leader of the Sages; he hands Rabbi Akiva the honor of the blessing, then rebukes him

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Recites the short blessing and defends it by Rabban Gamliel's own rule

terms.meaning: A short after-blessing that sums up in one paragraph the three main blessings of the full Grace after Meals.
The blessings said after eating a meal with bread.

10.note: The Sages kept praising the son of Rav Zevid to Rabbi Zeira as a great man and an expert in blessings, and Rabbi Zeira asked them to bring him when he came. When he visited and was served bread, he said the blessing with the word motzi rather than hamotzi. Rabbi Zeira was annoyed: is this the great expert they talk about? Had he said hamotzi he would have taught something, but saying motzi teaches nothing. The Gemara explains that he chose motzi to keep himself out of the dispute.
10.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Nehemya over whether the blessing on bread should say hamotzi or motzi. This story shows a scholar choosing the wording that is valid by every opinion.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who wants to meet the praised expert and is let down by his blessing

people.name: son of Rav Zevid
people.about: Brother of Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Zevid, praised by the Sages as an expert in blessings

terms.meaning: Two wordings of the blessing over bread, 'Who brings forth' or 'Who brought forth' bread from the earth; the Sages disputed which tense hamotzi carries, but all agree motzi means the past.
Jewish law; the ruling that is followed in practice.

11.note: Two students sat before bar Kappara when cooked cabbage, Damascene plums and young birds were served. Bar Kappara let one of them say the blessing, and he rushed to bless the birds first; the other student mocked him. Bar Kappara was angry. First he said he was angry not at the one who blessed but at the one who mocked: if your friend acts like someone who never tasted meat, why mock him? Then he said he was angry at the one who blessed: if there is no wisdom here, is there no elder here to ask? The teaching adds that neither of them lived out the year.
11.why: The Gemara has been asking which blessing goes on boiled vegetables, and it tries to read the two students' dispute as that same disagreement. It then rejects that reading and says they disagreed over whether the food one prefers or the more nourishing cabbage comes first.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A teacher before whom the students sit; he grows angry at both of them

people.name: two students
people.about: One blesses the birds first, the other mocks him; neither lives out the year

terms.meaning: Young birds, here served cooked as a dish.
An older scholar; bar Kappara means they should have asked him which blessing to say first.

12.note: Rav Hisda and Rav Hamnuna were at a meal and were served dates and pomegranates. Rav Hamnuna said the blessing on the dates first. Rav Hisda asked: don't you hold the rule that whatever comes first in the verse about the Land of Israel's produce comes first in blessing, and the pomegranate comes before the date? Rav Hamnuna answered that the date is second after the word land, in a land of olive oil and honey, while the pomegranate is fifth after it. Rav Hisda said in admiration: who will give us iron legs so that we can serve you and hear you?
12.why: The Gemara has been reading the verse praising the Land of Israel for the order of blessings and for legal measures. This story applies its rule about blessing order to an actual meal.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who questions why the dates were blessed before the pomegranates

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who blesses the dates first and explains why by counting from the word land

terms.meaning: In this verse, honey means dates, from which date honey is made, so the dates count as the second item after land.

13.note: Rav Yehuda was preparing his son's wedding at the house of Rav Yehuda bar Haviva when sweet dessert bread was served. He heard the people saying the blessing over bread, Who brings forth bread from the earth, and asked what that sound was. They said yes, that was their blessing, citing Rabbi Mona, and that Shmuel ruled like him. Rav Yehuda said they had it wrong: Shmuel said the law does not follow Rabbi Mona. They objected that he himself had quoted Shmuel saying the full bread blessing is said over wafers. He answered that the wafers were different, because a person had made his meal on them.
13.why: The Gemara is asking when sweet bread served as dessert counts as real bread; Rav Nahman has just said it does when it is eaten as a meal. Rav Yehuda's answer draws the same line.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage arranging his son's wedding who corrects the guests' blessing over dessert bread

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Haviva
people.about: The man at whose house the wedding preparations take place

people.name: Rabbi Mona
people.about: A Sage cited for the view that dessert bread gets the full blessing over bread

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on Rabbi Mona is in dispute between Rav Yehuda and the guests

terms.meaning: Sweetened, spiced baked goods eaten after a meal, like a pastry.
A legal device using shared food that lets people carry in a shared courtyard, or cook on a festival for Shabbat.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

14.note: Rava and Rabbi Zeira were guests at the house of the Exilarch. After the table had been cleared, a portion of food was sent to them from the Exilarch. Rava ate it and Rabbi Zeira did not. Rabbi Zeira asked him: don't you hold that once the table is cleared one may not eat? Rava answered that they depended on the Exilarch's table.
14.why: The Gemara is asking when a meal is over, so that eating more needs a new blessing; Rav Pappa has just said it is when the table is cleared. Rava's answer adds that guests' meals are not over while their host's is not.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who eats the food sent after the table was cleared

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who does not eat it and asks Rava why he did

people.name: the Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who hosts the two Sages

terms.meaning: In the Sages' time each diner ate from a small table that was taken away at the end of the meal, so removing it marked the meal's end.

15.note: When Rav died, his students followed his coffin. On the way back they decided to eat bread by the Dannak River. After eating, they sat and could not settle a question: does the mishna's rule on saying the blessing together apply only when diners recline, or also when they agreed beforehand to eat at a certain place? Rav Adda bar Ahava stood, turned his torn cloak around so the tear was behind him, and tore it again, saying: Rav is dead, and we have not learned the laws of Grace after Meals. Then an elder came, set the mishna against a teaching from the early Sages, and resolved it: since they said let us go and eat in such-and-such a place, it is as if they reclined.
15.why: The Gemara has just answered a contradiction between the mishna, which says only reclining makes a shared meal, and a teaching that sitting is enough: planning to eat at a named place counts. The story shows Rav's students stuck on that very question.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A great teacher whose death and funeral open the story

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: One of Rav's students, who tears his garment a second time in grief

people.name: an elder
people.about: An older man who resolves the students' question

terms.meaning: Diners in the Sages' time lay on couches for a formal meal; reclining together made it a shared meal with one blessing for all.
Tearing one's clothing is a Jewish sign of mourning.
The blessings said after a meal with bread.

16.note: Rav Pappa visited the house of Rav Huna son of Rav Ika, and they were served scented oil and a myrtle branch. Rav Pappa said the blessing over the myrtle first and then over the oil. Rav Huna asked whether he did not hold that the law follows Rabban Gamliel's deciding opinion, oil first. Rav Pappa replied that Rava had ruled like Beit Hillel. The Gemara says this was not so; Rav Pappa said it to get himself out of an awkward spot.
16.why: The Gemara has just cited a dispute over whether oil or myrtle is blessed first, with Rabban Gamliel deciding for oil and Rabbi Yohanan ruling that the law follows him. This story shows a Sage who acted against that ruling and how he excused himself.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A guest who blesses the myrtle before the oil

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Ika
people.about: The host, who questions Rav Pappa's order of blessings

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whom Rav Pappa claims ruled like Beit Hillel; the Gemara says he did not

terms.meaning: A fragrant plant; Jews say a blessing over pleasant smells, such as myrtle or scented oil.
The school of the Sage Hillel, which here says the myrtle is blessed before the oil.
Rabban Gamliel, who settled the dispute between the schools of Hillel and Shammai in favor of oil first.

17.note: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled going with Rabbi Yohanan to eat the fruit of Genosar. When a hundred of them went, each brought him ten fruits; when ten went, each brought a hundred, and every hundred filled a basket of three se'a. Rabbi Yohanan ate them all and would swear he had not had a proper meal. Rabbi Abbahu ate until a fly would slip off his forehead; Rav Ami and Rav Asi ate until their hair fell out; Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish ate until he became confused, and Rabbi Yohanan would tell the household of the Nasi, and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia would send officers to bring him home.
17.why: The mishna has said that salted food can be the main dish with bread secondary, and Rav Ashi explained that this was for people eating the very sweet fruit of Genosar. These tales show how sweet and plentiful that fruit was.

people.about: The Sage who tells of going with Rabbi Yohanan to eat Genosar fruit

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Eats until a fly would slip from his forehead

terms.meaning: A region by the Sea of Galilee famous for its very sweet fruit.
A measure of volume; a basket of three se'a is a large basket.
The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.

18.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting together when raw vegetables were served before the fourth hour of the day. Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate; Mar Zutra did not. They asked him whether he was following Rabbi Yitzhak's saying that one may not talk to a person who ate vegetables that early because of the smell, since he was talking to them anyway. He answered that he followed Rabbi Yitzhak's other saying: it is forbidden to eat raw vegetables before the fourth hour.
18.why: The Gemara has just quoted both of Rabbi Yitzhak's sayings about eating vegetables early in the day. This story shows Mar Zutra telling them apart.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who eats the raw vegetables

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who will not eat the raw vegetables and explains which rule he follows

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who eats the raw vegetables

terms.meaning: The fourth hour of the day, counted from daybreak, so roughly mid-morning.

19.note: Yehuda bar Mareimar, Mar bar Rav Ashi and Rav Aha of Difti ate bread together. None was greater than the others, so none was the obvious one to lead the blessing. They wondered whether the rule that three who eat together must join in a shared blessing applies only when one of them is a great man, and whether equals do better to bless separately. Each blessed for himself. Then they went to Mareimar, who told them they had fulfilled the blessing but not the zimmun, and that a zimmun cannot be done after the fact.
19.why: The Gemara has been discussing when diners must or may split up for the blessing after a meal, including a teaching that two learned people who ate together should bless separately. This story asks whether the same holds for three equals, and Mareimar's answer is no.

people.about: One of three equal scholars who eat together

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: One of the three

people.name: Rav Aha of Difti
people.about: One of the three

people.name: Mareimar
people.about: The Sage they ask afterward, who says they missed the zimmun

terms.meaning: The invitation to bless together: when three or more eat together, one invites the others to join in Grace after Meals.
The blessings said after a meal with bread.

20.note: Rabbi Zeira fell ill, and Rabbi Abbahu, visiting him, vowed that if the little man with the scorched legs, his nickname for Rabbi Zeira, recovered, he would make a feast for the Sages. Rabbi Zeira recovered and Rabbi Abbahu made the feast. When it was time to break bread, Rabbi Abbahu asked Rabbi Zeira to do it; Rabbi Zeira reminded him of Rabbi Yohanan's rule that the host breaks bread, and Rabbi Abbahu broke it. When it was time for Grace after Meals, Rabbi Abbahu asked Rabbi Zeira to lead it, and Rabbi Zeira cited Rav Huna of Babylonia: whoever breaks bread leads the blessing. The text does not say here who led it.
20.why: The Gemara has been discussing who should lead the blessings at a meal. It goes on to explain that Rabbi Abbahu followed the teaching that the host breaks bread and the guest leads Grace, so that the guest can bless the host.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Falls ill and recovers; the guest of honor at the feast

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Vows a feast for the Sages if Rabbi Zeira recovers, and hosts it

terms.meaning: Say the blessing over bread and cut it for everyone at the start of the meal.
The blessings said after a meal with bread.
